narrative:
The letter you started at the inn never quite got finished before news overtakes it - a carter fresh off the Aldenmoor road, recognizing your face from a market day years back, stops you outright.

@Carter: Same blight that's got the fields sick everywhere this season - it's reached your valley too. Heard it from your Elder Maren's own courier, matter of fact. Didn't want to be the one telling you, but better from me than not at all.

narrative: You already promised a stranger's messenger you'd look into sick fields on the next road over. Now your own valley needs the same kind of help, and you can't be in both places converging on the same season's disaster.

narrative: The road back feels shorter than the road out did, which makes no physical sense and every emotional one. Aldenmoor comes into view looking smaller than you remembered and exactly as familiar - except for the fields, patchy and yellowed the same way you've now seen twice on this same short journey.

narrative:
Elder Maren doesn't look surprised to see you, which somehow doesn't diminish how glad she seems about it.

@Elder Maren: The road taught you something already, I see - or brought you back before it could finish. Either way. The blight's the same one everyone's contending with this season, near as any of us can tell. Not unique to us. Small comfort, but a real one.

narrative: The east field is worse than you let yourself imagine on the road back - not ruined yet, but close enough that 'the same as everywhere else' stops being comforting the moment it's your own family's harvest doing the failing.

narrative:
You do for Aldenmoor exactly what you'd have wanted a stranger to do for any village on the road - divide the labor fairly, pool what little surplus exists, make sure no single household bears more than its share of a disaster nobody chose. It's not magic. It's just competence, applied with love instead of distance.

@Elder Maren, watching from the field's edge: There it is. That's what leaving taught you that staying wouldn't have. Good.

narrative:
Nessa doesn't look reassured, exactly, but something in her shoulders unknots slightly at the honesty rather than false comfort.

@Nessa: Okay. Okay, that's - that's actually better than if you'd just said it'll be fine. Nobody's said one true thing to me all week.

narrative:
Joss finds you mid-effort, wiping mud on trousers that have clearly given up looking presentable days ago.

@Joss: Look who couldn't stay away. I'm not going to make this weird by admitting I'm glad. So I won't. I'm just going to hand you this shovel and let the gladness stay implied.

narrativeVariants.flags.aldenmoor_organized == true:
Aldenmoor doesn't come through this season unscathed, but it comes through together, and the fair-shares system you organized outlasts the crisis itself - Elder Maren mentions, almost offhand, that the valley might keep doing it this way even once the blight's fully passed. Aveline finds you the morning you finally leave again.

@Aveline: Go on, then. Properly this time. You've more than earned the leaving - and left something behind worth more than you probably realize yet.

narrative:
You keep walking, and it costs more than the decision felt like it should when you made it. Every mile puts more distance between you and a valley that might genuinely need the hands you're choosing not to give it.

@You (to yourself, more than once): Elder Maren's handled worse without me. Aveline's handled worse without me. That's not the same as it being easy to believe at three in the morning.

narrative:
Word does reach you, eventually, days later, secondhand and imperfect the way news always is once it's traveled far enough - Aldenmoor weathered the blight, thinner and poorer for it but intact, Elder Maren and the valley's own stubbornness apparently sufficient where your presence would have been a comfort, not a necessity.

It's good news. It doesn't entirely feel like it, not at first, and that particular gap between the facts and the feeling turns out to be something you'll carry for a while yet.

narrative:
You find a rider willing to carry both coin and word to Aldenmoor for what feels like an unreasonable fee and pay it anyway, watching them go with the particular helplessness of having done something and still not knowing if it was the right something.

@You (in the letter, roughly): Use this however Elder Maren says is fairest. I'm sorry I'm not there to help carry it myself. I'll make it up properly when I can.

narrative:
A reply does eventually find you, in Elder Maren's own economical hand, three lines that manage to be both gracious and quietly pointed at once.

@Elder Maren's letter: The coin helped more than you'd think. So would you have, if you'd come. Both things are true; only one of them was possible this season, and you chose the other. I don't say that as blame - only so you know it was noticed, by more people than just me.
